subtitle: Folding a clause into a noun phrase, and unfolding it again
words.intro: Germany remembers on its pavements. Small brass stones, an empty library under a square, a plaque on a school wall. Official memory is written in noun phrases, and it pays to be able to open them.

grammar[0].fact: Noun style hides people, and that can be its purpose. A plain test for any German official sentence: ask *Wer?* If the text won’t tell you, consider why. Writers who care about this go back to verbs on purpose.

grammar[1].fact: On 10 May 1933 students burned books on what’s now Bebelplatz in Berlin. Under a glass pane in its paving is an empty underground library, with room for 20,000 books. It’s easy to walk across without noticing, and that’s part of its point.

document.intro: Two real bronze plates, set into the paving of Bebelplatz, beside the empty library below. Read them slowly. This is German with no adjective to spare, and with the verb where it needs to be.
document.fact: The Heine line on the left comes from a play of 1820, about the burning of books in Spain, more than a century before it happened here. Thousands of books were thrown on the fire that night, with a speaker calling out authors by name.

reading.intro: A small town wants to put a plaque on its old school, after sixty years of arguing. Vroni from the local paper has the draft. It is one sentence long. She has asked Frau Eder, who is 94 and was a pupil there, to read it. Frau Eder has asked for it to be read aloud.
reading.photos[1].caption: Der Platz von oben gesehen: fast leer, an einem gewöhnlichen Tag.
reading.fact: The artist Gunter Demnig began laying *Stolpersteine*, small brass stones set into the pavement outside the last home a victim chose freely, in the 1990s. There are now tens of thousands across Europe. *Stolpern* means to stumble: you stop, and you bow your head to read.
